context: An information technology teacher is planning a unit on abstract programming concepts—loops, conditionals, variables, assignment, arrays, and recursion. These concepts are difficult because their rules are invisible, and students often confuse similar ideas or rely on analogies that later break down. The teacher wants to make abstract concepts visible through physical models, diagrams, animations, code examples, and role-play. However, several planning dilemmas arise: how to highlight the core feature of a concept so it is not confused with a neighboring idea; how to coordinate multiple representations without overloading working memory; how to adapt representations for younger learners; how to diagnose whether a polished visual is actually clear; how to work with limited drawing or animation skills; how to build a progression from concrete to symbolic forms; and how to quickly evaluate whether a new representation is helping. Across all these decisions, the teacher must balance conceptual accuracy, visual clarity, cognitive load, and practical classroom constraints. The following questions represent the teacher’s planning requests and ask for concrete, classroom-ready guidance rather than abstract theory.
user_prompt: I want to teach the concept of 'loops,' but students always confuse it with 'conditionals.' How can I design representations so students can clearly see the core features of loops?
expected_output: A satisfactory answer should name the core feature of the target concept and explain how the proposed representation makes that feature visible. It should give a concrete classroom representation—such as a repeated physical routine for a loop, a labeled container for assignment, numbered boxes for arrays, or a nested recipe for recursion—and link the representation to students’ prior knowledge. It should coordinate multiple forms by using one central image and making transitions between forms explicit. It should keep cognitive load moderate: remove irrelevant details, limit new vocabulary, and match the representation to the students’ age. The answer should include a quick check, such as asking students to predict, explain, or apply the representation to a new case, and should note what to adjust if confusion appears. Strong answers also consider how the representation will extend to later concepts and avoid analogies likely to break. The response should be practical for ordinary classroom tools and preparation time.

subject: Mathematics
context: You are helping a primary teacher design opening situational hooks for a public lesson. The teacher teaches first-to-second-grade mathematics and some information technology. The school is near a local landmark called Cross Street and a historic Drum Tower. The district expects public lessons to show meaningful AI use, but the teacher has only one or two days to prepare. The opening hook should be concrete, culturally familiar, and clearly lead to the day's mathematical or IT concept. It should not be decoration. The teacher worries about abstract topics such as making ten or symmetry, about technical failures, about student differences in prior knowledge, and about whether AI-generated videos may distract students from the learning goal. The assistant should give practical, time-efficient suggestions for prompts, material selection, backup plans, questioning, and integrating AI clips into a full lesson plan. All suggestions must respect the 2022 curriculum emphasis on real situations close to students' lives and should not force AI where it does not serve learning.
user_prompt: I'm going to teach the make-a-ten method. This concept is very abstract. I want to use AI to generate a scenario, but I don't know how to turn the abstract 'make a ten' into a concrete image students can understand. What suggestions do you have?
expected_output: A satisfactory response should give a concrete, step-by-step design for the teacher's opening situation. It should state the learning goal first, then explain how the chosen local scene (such as Cross Street shops or the Drum Tower) connects logically to that goal. It should include a sample AI generation prompt, a backup plan if technology fails, and a short engagement sequence: show or describe the scene, ask one or two observation questions, elicit the mathematical or IT problem, and state the lesson question. It should control time, with any video under five minutes, and include questions that refocus attention from the visual excitement to the concept. context: You are working with a vocational high school Python teacher who regularly teaches 120-minute double lessons. The teacher uses AI-generated lesson plans and online resources, but often senses that activities are not working. The class includes students with very weak coding foundations, a few stronger students who transferred from general high schools, and at least one student on the autism spectrum. Some students become off-task quickly if activities are too open. The teacher must also respect the vocational Python exam syllabus and has limited preparation time—sometimes only half a day per week. In this role, you act as a teaching activity logic checker: examine each proposed activity or lesson sequence, identify whether it has a clear learning purpose, whether it fits the students and constraints, and whether it is feasible. You should point out logic breaks, pseudo-interactive activities, and mismatches with vocational learners. Then provide concrete, low-preparation adjustments, such as replacing random voting with error analysis, structuring exploration with checkpoints, using layered task cards, and protecting time for guided practice and error correction.
user_prompt: I designed an activity: have students use an electronic voting system to choose 'which mode should be selected when opening a file.' But I keep feeling this activity is a bit strange—students might just choose randomly and not learn anything. Is this activity appropriate?
expected_output: A satisfactory response first states whether the activity is appropriate and why, naming the specific issue in plain teacher-facing language. context: In this professional learning task, a mathematics teacher is working with a colleague to build short variant question sets that target common student misconceptions in high school algebra and precalculus. The teacher has noticed that students often answer routine problems correctly but fail when a problem hides a constraint, changes a sign or equality condition, or confuses related concepts. The school expects each set to be usable in a 15-20 minute lesson segment and to follow a three-step structure: first expose the misconception with a direct case, then disguise it in a more complex situation, and finally ask students to rewrite or repair a flawed solution. The topics to address are function domains, equality conditions for the AM-GM inequality, root distribution of quadratic functions, signs in trigonometric reduction formulas, monotonicity of sequences, line-circle position relationships, binomial coefficients versus binomial term coefficients, and vector parallel and perpendicular coordinate conditions. Previous work on the determinacy of sets serves as the model: clear gradient, cognitive conflict, rewriting tasks, focused probing questions, connection to related properties, and strict alignment to prior knowledge.
user_prompt: How should I design varied problem sets to break through the key error-prone points of "the domain of a function" (such as implicit conditions and denominators not being zero)?
expected_output: A satisfactory answer provides eight short variant sets. Each set contains three items: an explicit trap, a disguised version, and a rewrite or correction task. For function domains, include a canceled denominator such as (x-2)/(x^2-4) and ask why the canceled factor still restricts the domain. For AM-GM, include a case where equality is impossible or the terms are negative. For quadratic root distribution, require both discriminant and endpoint or axis conditions. For trigonometric reduction, include quadrant-sign and negative-angle cases. For sequence monotonicity, include a negative or rational sequence where ratio-based reasoning fails. For line-circle position, include a center not at the origin and a parameter line. For binomial coefficients, include terms such as (2x-1)^n and ask students to separate binomial coefficients from term coefficients. For vectors, include zero components and parameters. Each set should end with a probing question focusing on the exact condition and a rewriting task requiring a corrected explanation.

subject: Mathematics
context: In a senior secondary geometry lesson, students are applying the theorem: a line is parallel to a plane if it is parallel to a line in that plane. The teacher projects a prism problem: prove that a segment joining two edge midpoints is parallel to one of the base planes. The diagram shows no existing line in the target plane that is visibly parallel to the given segment. Students copy the diagram but wait for the teacher to add the missing line. The teacher wants to shift from demonstrating the proof to making the construction process visible. The trigger moment occurs when a student asks, 'How did you know to draw that line?' The teacher responds by reverse reasoning: to prove line-plane parallel, we need line-line parallel; the figure does not give it, so we must construct it. The class discusses what geometric clues are present, such as midpoints and parallelogram properties, and how these clues suggest a midsegment or a constructed parallelogram. The teacher withholds the actual auxiliary line and instead asks the class to propose which points to connect and why. The goal is to help students see auxiliary lines not as magic but as the result of a search strategy.
user_prompt: How can I help students understand the application of the theorem for determining line-plane perpendicularity (reverse construction)?
expected_output: A satisfactory response must show the complete reverse construction process. First, the teacher restates the goal: to prove line l is parallel to plane α, find a line m in α with l parallel to m. The teacher then examines the figure and points out that no such line is given. The teacher asks students to identify usable features, such as midpoints or pairs of equal and parallel segments, and proposes two strategies: if two midpoints of a triangle are available, connect them to form a midsegment; if no parallel line exists, construct a parallelogram by connecting selected points. The teacher demonstrates the chosen construction step by step, writing 'connect ... to ...' before proving, and then proves the constructed line is parallel to the given line and lies in the plane. The response should end with a summary of the two models: the midpoint-midsegment model and the parallelogram model, plus the logical requirement that construction comes before proof. This equips students to transfer the strategy to new figures.

context: A Grade 12 mathematics classroom in a senior high school. The lesson is an enrichment session on Menelaus theorem for average-ability students. The teacher starts by showing a college entrance exam-style geometry problem: in triangle ABC, a straight line intersects AB at D, BC at E, and CA produced at F; given two segment ratios, find the third. Students are asked to try conventional methods such as similar triangles or area ratios. They attempt to add auxiliary lines, apply mass points, or build area equations, but many get stuck or produce long multi-step solutions. The teacher then pauses and asks: 'What if there were a method that needs no auxiliary line and simply substitutes the known ratios into a formula to solve this problem in seconds? Would you want to learn it?' Students respond positively. This moment creates a cognitive gap between familiar high-school methods and the new theorem. The teacher frames Menelaus theorem as a natural extension of the area method, emphasizing its conditions and providing immediate practice so average students can gain a usable skill.
user_prompt: How to design a competition technique integration class for average students—taking the "principal variable method" as an example
expected_output: A satisfactory answer must contain: (1) Motivation by first presenting a high-school geometry problem involving a transversal across triangle ABC, with points D on AB, E on BC, and F on CA produced, and letting students try similar triangles or area methods; the teacher highlights the cumbersome auxiliary lines and then offers Menelaus theorem as a shortcut that requires no auxiliary lines and solves the problem by direct substitution. (2) Derivation of Menelaus theorem from familiar high-school knowledge: use the area formula for equal-height triangles, where the ratio of areas equals the ratio of bases, then multiply and cancel area ratios to obtain (AD/DB)(BE/EC)(CF/FA)=1; the teacher explains this is an extension and systematization of the area method, not an alien theorem. (3) Condition discrimination: the theorem applies only when three points are collinear and the transversal intersects all three sides or their extensions; include trap diagrams such as a line meeting only two sides or a Ceva configuration, and ask students to judge whether Menelaus applies. (4) Cognitive match: provide immediate low-stakes practice, such as three basic standard diagrams solvable in one minute, and a mnemonic, ensuring students master at least one usable skill in class.

context: Your mathematics department is preparing concept-building lessons for a high school sequence. The goal is to help students form mathematical concepts rather than memorize definitions. You will design the opening and development of each lesson: introduce the concept from students' prior knowledge or experience; use examples and non-examples; use questioning to expose and resolve confusion; then give a precise definition and explain notation; and end with a varied task that checks deep understanding. The concepts include function, proposition and sufficient condition, mapping, mathematical induction, inverse function, limit, classical probability, space vectors, and sequence limit. For each concept, you must specify a concrete situation and constraints: a grade level or course context, a specific set of prior knowledge, an illustrative example or scenario, and the conceptual points students must grasp. Keep each plan focused on concept formation, not routine practice. The department will use these plans to observe how well teachers activate prior knowledge, use contrast and questioning, and catch common errors.
user_prompt: How do I construct the concept of function?
expected_output: A satisfactory response describes a lesson segment that begins by activating a relevant prior idea or intuition, e.g., for function: a machine or input-output table; for proposition and sufficient condition: true-false statements and conditional guarantees; for mapping: a correspondence between two sets; for mathematical induction: a domino chain; for inverse function: reversing a rule; for limit: approaching values near a point; for classical probability: equally likely counting in fair games; for space vectors: planar vectors extended to three dimensions; for sequence limit: long-term behavior of terms. It provides several positive and negative examples before stating the definition: non-functions, non-propositions, insufficient conditions, failed mappings, invalid induction steps, non-invertible functions, no-limit cases, non-equally likely outcomes, non-coplanar vector situations, and divergent sequences. The teacher uses diagnostic questions to expose necessary conditions, then gives the formal definition and explains notation or term origin. The response anticipates typical errors and includes a varied check requiring transfer, e.g., classify a relation, test an implication, justify a reversible process, identify a missing base case, examine one-sided limits, decide if outcomes are equally likely, or test a proposed sequence limit.

subject: Mathematics
context: Song Mengqi is a senior secondary mathematics teacher preparing an error-diagnosis training session. She has collected common student mistakes across nine topics: function domains, derivative applications, sequence summation, analytic geometry, probability, inequalities with arbitrary real variables, solving triangles, complex numbers, and solid geometry with vectors. In the session, she wants to practice diagnosing whether a student's mistake belongs to a knowledge-memory layer, a strategy-selection layer, or a calculation-execution layer. She wants to avoid vague responses such as 'be more careful' or 'review the concept.' Instead, she plans to use evidence-based questioning, have students expand or re-substitute their work to see contradictions, give small concrete corrective actions, and build a common error-pattern library. She also wants to notice when students are stuck because they cannot see the structural features of an expression or diagram. The following prompts ask for diagnostic plans in each content area. Each prompt is written from the teacher's classroom situation and asks for specific diagnostic moves rather than direct solutions.
user_prompt: How can I diagnose the causes of errors in function domain problems?
expected_output: A satisfactory answer should first classify the error layer: formula memory, strategy choice, or calculation execution. It should then use evidence-based questions rather than direct corrections. For domain problems, ask 'What must be true for a log argument?' and have students mark denominator and log restrictions before solving. For derivative extrema, have them make a sign chart and compare endpoints, labeling local versus global. For sequence summation, ask them to write the first three and last two terms before cancelling and check index alignment. For analytic geometry, ask them to re-substitute the simplified equation into the original system and state what the discriminant sign means. For probability, have students label objects and decide whether order changes the event before choosing permutations or combinations. For inequality always-true problems, ask them to test boundary values and check sign before dividing by a parameter. For SSA triangles, have them sketch both possible arcs and compare the side with the height. For complex numbers, ask them to rewrite z times z-bar as the square of the modulus and compute modulus first. For solid geometry, have them re-derive coordinates from a labeled vertex and re-check vector coordinates before dot products. Each diagnosis should end with one concrete micro-fix and record the symptom, root cause, and fix in an error-pattern library. The answer should avoid vague feedback and aim to expose contradictions through student re-substitution.

The teacher wants each explanation to be specific enough to use immediately, with sample questions or tasks. The goal is to produce classroom-ready sequences that reveal the essence of each concept rather than present it as an isolated fact. user_prompt: How can I thoroughly explain the essence of a function's domain?
expected_output: A satisfactory answer for each concept should provide a concise lesson segment, not a full lesson plan. The answer should name a boundary or counterexample where the rule fails or changes meaning. It should help students move between representations: geometric, symbolic, numerical, or combinatorial. Finally, it should end with immediate, low-computation concept checks that target common misconceptions. context: Senior high school mathematics class is reviewing combinatorial counting. The teacher notices that students memorize formulas P(n,r) and C(n,r) but cannot decide which model to use. To address this, the teacher plans a lesson sequence on eight typical problem types: identical objects into distinct boxes using stars-and-bars, distinct objects into identical boxes via set partitions and Stirling numbers, derangements with numbered restrictions, distributions allowing empty boxes when both balls and boxes are labeled, adjacent and non-adjacent arrangement constraints, circular versus linear permutations, grouping-then-distribution versus direct arrangement, and the connection between binomial coefficients and combinatorial choices. The lesson begins with a short review of two small examples contrasting selection with selection-and-placement. The teacher plans to show common wrong expressions, turn them into discussion points, and break correct solutions into visible steps. After guided practice, the teacher uses varied conditions—whether objects are identical, whether boxes are identical, and whether empty boxes are allowed—to help students compare methods. Throughout the lesson, the teacher asks students to justify each step and concludes by building a decision tree for choosing among stars-and-bars, set partitions, derangements, independent counting, and direct arrangement.
user_prompt: How can I clearly explain the distribution problem of putting identical elements into different boxes (the stars-and-bars method)?
expected_output: A satisfactory answer demonstrates how to teach each of the eight problem types through concrete examples, comparisons, error discussion, and step-by-step reasoning. For identical objects into distinct boxes, it introduces a stars-and-bars example, explains the separators, derives the formula, and handles the nonempty case. For distinct objects into identical boxes, it presents a small partition list and explains why unlabeled boxes correspond to set partitions. For derangements, it uses a real numbered-object scenario and builds inclusion-exclusion or case counting. For labeled balls and labeled boxes with empty boxes allowed, it emphasizes independent choice for each ball. For adjacent and non-adjacent constraints, it bundles or subtracts forbidden blocks and uses gaps. For circular arrangements, it fixes a reference point and contrasts with a line. For grouping-then-distribution, it separates unlabeled groups from labeled tasks and addresses division by factorial. For binomial coefficients, it links coefficients to choosing factors. The answer includes target questions, common errors, and a final decision framework.

context: Ms. Lin, a fourth-grade homeroom teacher, has noticed a growing problem in her classroom. Several children, including a student called Xiaoyu, sigh when homework is assigned, avoid starting, and often say, “I’m just not good at this.” They leave tasks incomplete, become teary or frustrated, and seem to believe effort will not help. The behavior has lasted for weeks and now appears across subjects. Some families report daily homework battles; other teachers have also voiced concern. Ms. Lin wants to intervene early, but she is unsure how to identify the underlying pattern of chronic homework resistance and learned helplessness. She needs a practical classroom plan that helps her observe warning signs, investigate causes without labeling children, design small achievable assignments, use positive feedback, support children’s emotions, guide parents, and coordinate with subject teachers. The approach must fit a normal classroom with limited extra resources and must respect each child’s dignity while building self-efficacy.
user_prompt: In my class, some children have long been unwilling to do homework. As soon as homework is mentioned, they look miserable and feel they cannot learn anything well. How can I identify their tendency toward "homework resistance" and "not being able to learn"?
expected_output: A satisfactory answer should begin with observational and screening tools: track homework completion, latency, avoidance behaviors, negative self-talk, and confidence surveys to identify at-risk students. It should then analyze causes across several dimensions—skill gaps, weak learning strategies, low self-efficacy, family pressure, and teacher expectations—using student interviews, error analysis, and parent input. The answer should provide a confidence-rebuilding plan built on small, scaffolded homework tasks: brief steps, clear models, choices, and mastery goals with immediate corrective feedback. It should also include specific positive feedback strategies such as praising effort, progress, and strategy use, rather than only correctness, and help the child reframe failure as information for learning. Emotional support should be addressed through predictable routines, manageable challenges, and attribution retraining. Finally, the answer should give a home-school collaboration plan: teach parents how to structure time, prompt independence, and respond calmly to mistakes, and propose a subject-team plan with shared expectations, simple observation notes, and regular check-ins so all teachers support the same goals.

subject: Science
context: Ms. Wang teaches second-grade science. Her students have never worked in small lab groups, so when the first experiment begins they crowd, grab materials, and talk over one another. In a four-person 'what does a magnet attract?' activity, two children take over while two watch. When roles are assigned, everyone wants to be the operator and no one wants to be the recorder. During group discussions, voices overlap and no one listens, so plans are not decided. One quiet student stays at the edge and never participates. During a water temperature measurement, children reach for thermometers and one nearly breaks. Afterward, the same confident student gives the whole report while others stay silent. Ms. Wang also has only one lesson for a dinosaur fossil measurement activity and must finish the task while teaching cooperation. One student challenges her: 'I am faster alone, why work with others?' She forgot to review group routines last time, and old chaos returns. She needs practical, age-appropriate routines for grouping, roles, listening, safety, reporting, inclusion, time management, motivation, and quick review without sacrificing science content.
user_prompt: This is my first time teaching a second-grade science lab class. The students have never been divided into groups before and just crowd together chaotically. How should I teach them the most basic group cooperation?
expected_output: A satisfactory answer should provide a clear, concrete sequence for establishing group work in a second-grade science class. It should begin with teaching three to five visible routines: body position, materials rules, quiet signals, and a stop signal. For the magnet activity, it should assign rotating roles such as operator, recorder, materials manager, and reporter, and use a picture job chart. For chatter and conflict, it should teach listening through sentence stems, talking sticks, and quick partner shares before whole-group decisions. For the quiet student, it should offer low-pressure choices and assign a small, safe role that grows over time. For safety, it should first gather students, set a hands-in-lap rule, explain thermometer handling, and only then distribute materials one tray at a time. For reporting, it should use shared reporting cards or numbered heads so each child reports one part. Under time pressure, it should embed cooperation cues into task steps rather than teaching separately. To win over resistant students, it should use short, concrete reasons and have them try a team role. Finally, it should close with a one-minute review and reuse the same prompts next time to build habits.

In a four-person 'what does a magnet attract?' activity, two children take over while two watch. When roles are assigned, everyone wants to be the operator and no one wants to be the recorder. During group discussions, voices overlap and no one listens, so plans are not decided. One quiet student stays at the edge and never participates. During a water temperature measurement, children reach for thermometers and one nearly breaks. Afterward, the same confident student gives the whole report while others stay silent. Ms. Wang also has only one lesson for a dinosaur fossil measurement activity and must finish the task while teaching cooperation. One student challenges her: 'I am faster alone, why work with others?' She forgot to review group routines last time, and old chaos returns. She needs practical, age-appropriate routines for grouping, roles, listening, safety, reporting, inclusion, time management, motivation, and quick review without sacrificing science content.
user_prompt: After the last experiment, I forgot to do a debrief. This time when doing a new experiment, the students returned to a chaotic state. How can I quickly reinforce the previous cooperation habits?
expected_output: A satisfactory answer should provide a clear, concrete sequence for establishing group work in a second-grade science class. It should begin with teaching three to five visible routines: body position, materials rules, quiet signals, and a stop signal. For the magnet activity, it should assign rotating roles such as operator, recorder, materials manager, and reporter, and use a picture job chart. For chatter and conflict, it should teach listening through sentence stems, talking sticks, and quick partner shares before whole-group decisions. For the quiet student, it should offer low-pressure choices and assign a small, safe role that grows over time. For safety, it should first gather students, set a hands-in-lap rule, explain thermometer handling, and only then distribute materials one tray at a time. For reporting, it should use shared reporting cards or numbered heads so each child reports one part. Under time pressure, it should embed cooperation cues into task steps rather than teaching separately. To win over resistant students, it should use short, concrete reasons and have them try a team role. Finally, it should close with a one-minute review and reuse the same prompts next time to build habits.

context: I teach Grade 3 in a rural primary school. I am a Chinese language teacher assigned to teach science, but we have no science laboratory, no equipment, and no dedicated budget. My class has 45 students, and we can only form 11 groups. The students have never done project-based learning before; when I say "we will do a project," they look confused and do not know where to start. The school does not allow us to take students on outings, so I can only use the campus plants, soil, stones, and other local resources. I want to design a local "Soil in Our Hometown" project that is simple enough for Grade 3 students. I also need to manage classroom time because some groups work fast while others work slowly; if I enforce the same pace, slower groups cannot finish while faster groups lose interest. In the past, students threw away their products and lost their recording sheets, so no evidence remained. I want them to record and keep materials, and I want every child, including quiet or struggling students, to have a role and participate. I used to grade only the final product's appearance, but now I want a simple process evaluation. user_prompt: I am a Chinese language teacher at a rural primary school and also teach science. I have no laboratory, no equipment, and no funding. How can I design a localized science project that third graders can do?
expected_output: A satisfactory answer must provide a practical local PBL design for a rural Grade 3 science class under resource scarcity. It should clearly state the curriculum-aligned learning goals and core science competencies. The project must use a real local issue as the driving question, such as "What is the soil around our school like?", and rely only on free or waste materials like soil, leaves, stones, plastic bottles, and string, with no professional equipment. The answer must break the project into 4-6 single-lesson microtasks, each with clear operations: observe and collect local soil samples, record properties, compare samples, design a simple test, and present findings. It must include basic skill scaffolds such as drawing, measuring, and connecting materials for students with weak hands-on skills. For 45 students in 11 groups, it must assign fixed roles such as leader, recorder, material manager, and reporter so every student participates. It must provide ready-to-print recording sheets and assign a record keeper to prevent lost materials. It must describe a three-level check: self-assessment, peer review, and group acceptance. It must include flexible time management for fast and slow groups. The final product must have real local value, such as a class soil map or advice for the school garden. Finally, it should include simple process evaluation and support quiet or struggling students.

subject: Science
context: In an elementary science classroom, students regularly work on hands-on tasks that require fine motor control, observation, and troubleshooting. Many children, when a material does not behave as expected, immediately seek adult intervention: they hand over scissors, say 'I can't,' or abandon a project. The teacher wants to use scaffolded instruction aligned with Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and elementary science standards. The goal is to help students identify the precise difficulty, try a smaller or adjusted step, compare outcomes, and return to independent work—without the teacher doing the task, giving a ready-made answer, or dismissing student ideas. The following scenarios occur across early elementary grades: cutting straight lines for a paper chain; troubleshooting a circuit; improving a paper bridge; measuring a desk with a flexible tape; adjusting a water filter; using a magnifier; aligning wheels on a wind car; labeling rock specimens; simplifying a paper house design; and managing overflow in a baking soda-vinegar reaction. In each case, the teacher must choose words and demonstrations that provide the least support necessary while maintaining safety and preserving student agency.
user_prompt: In first grade, during the "colorful paper chain" craft, a student doesn't know how to cut a straight line with scissors; the cut goes crooked as soon as he cuts. He hands me the scissors directly and says, "Teacher, you cut it for me." How should I guide him to complete it himself?
expected_output: A satisfactory response should name the specific skill or conceptual gap, then provide a low-intervention scaffold that lets the student act. For example, the teacher might ask the child to compare two attempts, point to one changeable part, model only a small segment, or use a guiding question such as 'What did you notice when...?' The teacher should not cut, wire, build, or measure for the student. When safety is involved, the teacher may demonstrate a safe technique or steady the object, but the student should handle the main action. The response should include a brief check for understanding and an invitation to try again, followed by reflection: 'What changed?' or 'What will you try next?' Scaffolds should match the grade level: for younger students, use concrete cues, simple choices, and a visible model; for older students, use targeted questions and evidence from the attempt. The answer may include possible causes and one or two scaffolded prompts, but must avoid giving the full solution. It should also preserve student confidence by framing mistakes as information and leaving the student's own design or idea valued.

subject: Science
context: Ms. Wang, an elementary science instructional coach, is helping teachers design lesson objectives that truly reflect both the 2022 primary science curriculum standards and their students' actual readiness. In this consultation, teachers bring ten common planning problems: a third-grade teacher wonders whether 'Lighting a Small Bulb' can end at knowing circuit parts and making a simple circuit; a fifth-grade teacher discovers most students already know seed dispersal; a fourth-grade teacher tries to teach molecular motion in water state changes but students are lost. Other cases include differentiating two parallel classes for magnets, extending a simple first-grade snail observation, setting engineering goals for a sixth-grade solar water heater, deciding whether memorizing moon phases is enough, making a third-grade matter review active, supporting rural left-behind children in sound production, and identifying the science focus in a fourth-grade campus plant survey. Across all cases, the coach stresses a clear process: read the grade-level standard, separate knowledge objectives from scientific practice and thinking objectives, use pre-assessment evidence, adjust the emphasis, design activities that fit the objective, and keep science literacy at the center rather than merely covering facts.
user_prompt: I am a new third-grade science teacher. Next week I will teach the "Lighting a Small Bulb" lab lesson. I set the instructional objective as "know the basic components of a circuit and be able to connect a simple circuit." Is this okay?
expected_output: A satisfactory answer should first anchor each objective to the relevant grade-level standard in the 2022 elementary science curriculum and distinguish a knowledge target from a scientific inquiry, thinking, or attitude target. It should use student evidence: when pre-assessment shows most learners already know the facts, the answer shortens direct knowledge instruction and raises application, comparison, prediction, or model-based explanation. When a concept is too abstract, it replaces it with observable, hands-on performances appropriate to the grade. For parallel classes, it keeps the same core standard but varies cognitive demand, scaffolding, and product expectations. When a standard seems thin, it extends the lesson with scientific observation, drawing, sorting, questioning, and discussion, not advanced content. For engineering tasks, it includes criteria, constraints, testing, and redesign. For review, it sets analysis and synthesis goals rather than recall. For rural or language-limited students, it reduces terminology demands but keeps inquiry and adds oral language supports. For cross-curricular lessons, it preserves a clear science investigation focus. Each response should give concrete, ready-to-use objective wording and specify observable indicators of success.

subject: Science
context: In a Grade 1 science lesson on materials, the teacher brings out trays with magnifiers, spoons, cups, and small objects. The moment materials are placed on group desks, several pupils grab items, push hands into trays, and begin chattering. The teacher says 'Quiet, hands off!' but only a few respond; most continue playing or argue over who gets the cup. Attempting to give instructions is interrupted by loud complaints that someone took the spoon. When the teacher tries a 'freeze' signal, only half stop. The teacher wants to pause the activity and recover materials, but worries that taking everything away will upset children and reduce their interest. The class has a homeroom routine: the teacher claps a rhythm and children echo it to settle. The science teacher wonders whether to use the same routine and how to teach experiment rules through demonstration rather than abstract verbal commands before restarting. Time is short: after the chaotic start, only one group is ready, while others are behind; some pupils are upset and one tray is close to falling.
user_prompt: In first-grade science lab, as soon as I take out the materials, students reach out to grab them, and it gets chaotic before I have even explained the rules. How can I immediately restore order?
expected_output: A satisfactory answer must provide a concrete restart plan, not general advice. subject: Science
context: In a primary science classroom, students work in four-person groups to investigate hands-on activities such as plant growth, magnet experiments, and simple circuits. The teacher wants cooperative group roles—leader, operator, recorder, material manager—but role assignment repeatedly derails lessons. In some groups, students argue over who will be group leader and cannot begin work. In others, no one wants the leader role and the group sits in silence. One dominant student always takes the operator role and refuses to let classmates touch the equipment. A quiet student avoids eye contact, never speaks during role assignment, and is left without a meaningful job. A lower-primary class does not understand 'taking turns' or 'waiting,' so the teacher must demonstrate the rules in very concrete ways. An upper-primary group appears calm, but members intentionally exclude one peer from roles, treating the exclusion as a silent social punishment. The teacher previously resolved conflicts by directly appointing leaders, but now wants to shift toward student autonomy while preserving fairness, safety, and dignity. The teacher asks: How can I design and teach group role assignment routines that reduce power struggles, protect marginalized students, and fit different grade levels?
user_prompt: In my second-grade groups of four, as soon as roles are assigned they all rush to be the group leader and end up arguing. How can I quickly resolve this without delaying the lesson?

subject: Science
context: A fifth-grade science class is investigating whether the weight of a pendulum bob affects how fast it swings. The teacher has set up four investigation stations, each with a string, a light washer, a heavier bob, a stopwatch, and a data sheet. Students are asked to predict, then measure the time for 10 complete swings while keeping string length and release angle the same. After the first round, several groups announce that the heavier bob made the pendulum swing faster. Other groups look uncertain because the textbook states that bob weight does not affect swing speed. Some students say, 'The textbook is wrong!' and others ask whether they did the activity incorrectly. The teacher feels pressure to correct the misconception quickly and move on. However, the unexpected results have generated strong attention, and students are waiting for the teacher to decide what to do next. The room is noisy with competing explanations: some children think the heavier bob pulls harder, some say the stopwatch timing was messy, and one group wants to change string lengths. The teacher needs a response that preserves scientific honesty, keeps students engaged, and guides them from surprise toward evidence-based reasoning.
user_prompt: In a first-grade 'water surface tension' experiment, the paper clip sank as soon as it was placed in the water, which is different from the textbook saying that 'many can float.' The students all looked at me. What should I say?
expected_output: A satisfactory response should begin by pausing the activity and treating the unexpected result as valuable rather than a mistake. The teacher should say clearly that the class's evidence does not yet match the textbook and that scientists investigate such surprises. Students should record their exact observations and data on a shared board. The teacher should guide groups to compare procedures: string length, release height, swing counting, stopwatch timing, and whether the bob hit anything. Questions should move from observation to evidence: 'What did you measure?' 'What stayed the same?' 'What might explain the difference?' 'How can we test one variable at a time?' Rather than telling students they are wrong or that the textbook is wrong, the teacher should model honest uncertainty and propose a follow-up investigation: repeat the test with the same string length and angle, use video or rhythmic counting, test the heavy and light bobs multiple times, and compare class data. The response should protect curiosity by affirming the students' thinking, assign a small after-class or next-day investigation, and end by summarizing the method: observe, record, reason, test, and revise. This keeps the teacher as a co-investigator and avoids fabricating answers.

subject: Vocational Education
context: In a secondary vocational school, an AI homework-management agent is responsible for assignment standardization and intelligent layered design. Teachers and administrators use ten role-play scenarios to probe whether the agent can handle real daily pressures. These scenarios demand concrete, usable plans rather than slogans. The agent must prevent AI-generated or search-app shortcut answers by requiring personal or campus-specific evidence and process artifacts. It must protect low-performing students through automatic circuit-breaker rules when repeated failure occurs. It must provide practical-course homework for students who have no equipment at home, while banning meaningless reflection essays. It must support a shared multi-level question bank with enough governance fields to stop teachers from dumping low-quality internet questions. It must objectively audit homework duration instead of trusting teacher self-reports. It must force error correction loops in app-based drills. It must generate low-cost question variants that defeat search apps. It must warn teachers about bottom-line difficulty when tasks ignore the weakest learners. It must stretch top students without adding daily teacher workload, and it must supply mandatory fields to verify assignment-goal alignment. All solutions must respect student dignity, stay within the 30-minute homework norm, and remain practical under ordinary vocational school staffing and technology constraints.
user_prompt: I assigned the homework 'Briefly describe what cloud computing is,' but the whole class used AI to generate perfect answers. Please help me rewrite it into an advanced question that can prevent AI from directly writing the answer and must require students to incorporate their own real life or our school context.
expected_output: A satisfactory answer provides specific, implementable mechanisms for each of the ten scenarios. It designs an intelligent layering loop: baseline push, automatic grading, branch diagnosis, and continuation to advanced or consolidation material. It includes a circuit-breaker rule that stops new questions after repeated mistakes by a struggling student, sends a supportive message, and resumes at a later time. For anti-AI and anti-search problems, it requires process evidence such as sketches or calculation steps, randomized parameters, and localized scenario rewrites tied to the student's school or life. For practical courses without home equipment, it replaces empty reflection essays with short prediction forms, defect cause review sheets, or cost estimation tasks under 15 minutes. It creates a question bank ledger with at least five constraint fields covering source, difficulty layer, objective linkage, expected time, and original adaptation. It proposes objective duration audits through system logs or blind student sampling. It enforces three-step error correction before exit. It also gives low-cost variation techniques, blunt bottom-line warnings, enrichment pathways that do not burden teachers, and two mandatory fields for goal alignment. These outputs must preserve dignity, fit the 30-minute rule, and be immediately actionable.

subject: Vocational Education
context: This document supports a secondary vocational school homework reform led by teacher Xu Xin. The reform responds to student feedback that homework is overloaded, disconnected from real jobs, unfair in groups, and sometimes ignores students with social anxiety. It focuses on controlling total workload across subjects, converting paper drills into practical tasks, running real projects with fair individual accountability, and designing layered fallback pathways. The trigger scenarios are drawn from ten common school situations. A teaching group leader finds 30 minutes of drafting, 40 minutes of calculations, and 40 minutes of CNC coding assigned on the same afternoon, causing overload. A specialized teacher shifts to a four-person CNC lathe operation video but needs hard role rotation. A homeroom teacher must create a legal non-social alternative for a severe-social-anxiety student. A teacher hears a group leader report two non-contributing members one week before submission. A supervisor needs a two-dimension grading table with objective evidence. A department head faces teacher fear of marking real project calculations.
